newsitem.title: USA: Oregon electricity restructure bill takes form.
newsitem.headline: Oregon electricity restructure bill takes form.

text.p: Legislation to restructure Oregon's electricity industry has begun to take shape, but areas of disagreement remain after a key state committee reviewed a proposed consensus bill on Thursday.

The Oregon House of Representative's Committee on Power Deregulation will hold the first of several public hearings on the bill to allow competition by January 1, 2000, next Tuesday, said John Larson, administrator of the committee.
He said he expects a full House vote on a final measure in May.
The bill, which will be folded into an existing bill redefining public utilities to exclude power generators and suppliers who are not utilities, "still needs some fixes," Larsen noted.

Major areas of contention are said to be funding for public purpose interests, transition cost recovery, whether restructuring should be implemented separately for investor-owned utilities and public utility districts, and continued access to federal power for residential and small businesses consumers.
The bill contains provisions for current electricity suppliers to buy power from Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), the giant federal power agency serving the Northwest.
A portion of BPA's power traditionally has been guaranteed to smaller consumers in the region.
But some parties, such as Enron Corp, which plans to acquire Portland General Electric Co, object to that clause, Larsen said.
The bill also provides for a three percent bill surcharge for the funding of conservation and renewable energy programs.
But there is disagreement over how the fund should be administered, with consumer groups objecting to plans allowing utilities to take responsibility for the spending.

The issue for recovery of transition costs - roughly defined as investments made by regulated monopoly utilities which are likely to become uneconomic under market competition - is "all or some," Larsen said.
Under the proposed bill, the Oregon Public Utility Commission (OPUC) would be responsible for determining the amount of transition costs as well as how they would be recovered.
Utilities want to recover 100 percent of their uneconomic investments through rates, while consumer groups argue shareholders should also bear some of these costs.
OPUC oversight of the issue is also troubling to some, including Enron and Portland General, who view it as another form of re-regulation, Larsen said.
The bill will require a three-fifths majority of votes in the Oregon House before moving on to the State Senate and the governor's office.

At Thursday's hearing, Oregon Governor John Kitzhaber expressed support for the legislation, but made clear it depended on retaining access to BPA power, not empowering utilities to recover all stranded costs and strong provisions for consumer protection and cost-based rates, Larsen said.
